query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings used at high temperatures, wear resistance is governed by the formation of a self-adaptive ultra‐nanocrystalline, partially amorphous near-surface layer that develops during wear. This dynamic transformation reduces friction and inhibits crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin film with a nanocrystalline grain structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a high-temperature annealing pre-treatment designed to promote grain boundary mobility and enhance the propensity for dynamic amorphization during subsequent wear at elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted at high temperatures (approximately 500–700°C) under controlled sliding loads typical for protective coatings in high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline and partially amorphous surface layer acting as a mediator for reducing shear strength at worn interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding, enhanced grain boundary diffusion facilitates reorganization into a nanostructured amorphous layer. This layer can lower friction coefficients and resist the propagation of micro-cracks, thereby reducing the overall wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, annealed coatings will develop a stable ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer during wear testing that exhibits lower friction coefficients and wear rates compared to as‐deposited coatings.
generation.baseline: Standard as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin films without prior thermal pre-treatment.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective under high-temperature (500–700°C) sliding conditions; effects may not be observable at lower temperatures or under significantly different loading regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing parameters and the precise temperature range over which the surface layer forms most effectively remain uncertain, as does the extent to which the coating’s initial nanostructure influences the dynamic transformation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings: one set to undergo a high-temperature annealing pre-treatment and a control set in the as-deposited state. Subject both sets to wear testing at about 600°C under identical sliding load conditions. Monitor the evolution of the near-surface microstructure using high-resolution SEM, TEM, and XRD.
measurements: Surface microstructure (grain size, amorphous layer formation) via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the annealed coatings do not develop a measurable ultra‐nanocrystalline/partially amorphous surface layer or if there is no significant improvement in wear resistance and friction reduction compared to the as-deposited coatings under high-temperature conditions.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
